Nutrition

High-protein Indian vegetarian foods, and how to eat enough

A typical Indian vegetarian plate is built on roti, rice and a katori of dal, which adds up to far less protein than most people think. Here is how much the common foods actually give you, and how to build a day that is enough for the gym.

By Khushi Gupta · Reviewed October 2026 · 3 min read

On this page

  1. How much protein do you need?
  2. Protein in common vegetarian foods
  3. A 100 g vegetarian day, without supplements
  4. Tips that make it easier

How much protein do you need?

The ICMR-NIN recommended allowance for Indian adults is 0.83 g of protein per kg of body weight a day. That is the minimum to stay healthy, not the amount that builds muscle best.

For people who lift weights, a 2018 meta-analysis (Morton et al., British Journal of Sports Medicine) found muscle gain levelled off at about 1.6 g per kg a day, with some people benefiting from up to 2.2 g.

Body weightMinimum (0.83 g/kg)Lifting (1.6 g/kg)
50 kg42 g80 g
60 kg50 g96 g
70 kg58 g112 g
80 kg66 g128 g

Your own number is one click away in the protein calculator.

Protein in common vegetarian foods

Values are approximate. Dal and rajma are given cooked, per katori made from about 30 g of dry dal, because that is how they are eaten.

FoodServingProteinCalories
Soya chunks (dry)50 g26 g175 kcal
Paneer (full fat)100 g18 g265 kcal
Tofu (firm)100 g12-15 g120-145 kcal
Hung curd / Greek yogurt150 g12-15 g130-150 kcal
Whey protein1 scoop (30 g)24 g120 kcal
Milk (toned)250 ml8 g145 kcal
Dal, rajma or chole (cooked)1 katori7 g120-160 kcal
Besan50 g11 g195 kcal
Roasted chana30 g6 g110 kcal
Peanuts30 g7.5 g170 kcal
Sattu40 g8 g160 kcal
Curd (dahi)1 katori (150 g)5 g90 kcal
Roti (medium)13 g110 kcal
Cooked rice1 cup (150 g)4 g195 kcal

Two things stand out. Soya chunks, paneer, hung curd and tofu carry most of the load. Dal is a good food, but one katori gives about 7 g: you would need more than ten katoris to reach 80 g from dal alone.

A 100 g vegetarian day, without supplements

This day is roughly 1,900 kcal, which suits a lightly active 60 to 70 kg person. Scale the portions up or down with the calorie calculator.

MealWhat to eatProtein
Breakfast2 besan chillas (60 g besan) with 150 g hung curd26 g
Lunch2 roti, 1 katori rajma, soya chunk sabzi (30 g dry), salad28 g
Snack30 g roasted chana, 1 glass toned milk14 g
Dinner100 g paneer bhurji, 1 roti, 1 katori dal28 g
Totalabout 96-100 g

Add a scoop of whey or another 50 g of soya and you are comfortably at 120 g, enough for a 75 kg lifter.

Tips that make it easier

  • Put a protein food in every meal, not just at dinner. Three or four servings of 25 to 30 g work better than one big one.
  • Swap regular curd for hung curd. Straining it overnight roughly doubles the protein per spoon.
  • Use soya chunks in pulao, sabzi or keema-style dishes. 50 g dry gives as much protein as 140 g of paneer, for fewer calories.
  • Watch the paneer calories. It is high in fat, so on a fat loss diet, low-fat paneer or tofu goes further.
  • Mix dal with rice or roti. Grains and pulses together give a complete set of amino acids.

If you eat eggs, two eggs add about 12 g of protein for 140 kcal, one of the cheapest ways to close the gap.

Frequently asked questions

Can vegetarians build muscle without eggs or meat?

Yes. Muscle growth depends on total protein, training and calories, not on where the protein comes from. Vegetarians just have to plan more, leaning on soya, paneer, hung curd, tofu and, if they like, whey.

Which Indian vegetarian food has the most protein?

Dry soya chunks, at about 52 g per 100 g. Among everyday foods, paneer, tofu, hung curd and besan are the next best.

Is soya safe for men?

Yes, in normal food amounts. Studies have not found that eating soya foods lowers testosterone in men. One or two servings a day is a sensible amount.

Do I need whey protein as a vegetarian?

No, but it helps. One scoop gives about 24 g of protein for very few calories, which makes a high target much easier to reach on a budget or a busy day.
